name: Aaron Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the crew that builds and repairs the electricity company’s lines outside town. My two-year technical diploma gave me the drawings, but the apprenticeship taught me to hold a tester on the wire before saying a job is safe. I enjoy bringing younger workers along; I do not enjoy changing a sound method because a manager likes a new screen. My wife Elise and I have grown children, roughly four months of expenses saved and no firm retirement date. My pay is about usual for this job, and I have never used AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew to let the office shorten its forms, as long as a lineworker still signs the isolation result. A tidy page does not make a circuit dead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This mild version would leave my pay and shifts alone, and four months saved gives Elise and me some breathing room. I would not rush to learn a new tool for a few minutes of paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same repair checks and compare the new form with my switching notebook. During the first year I would send back any form that hides the test reading, then carry on with the scheduled crew jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Retirement can stay a family decision rather than a reaction to office stationery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you send the form back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the switching point and meter value cannot be found at a glance, the next crew is left guessing. I would mark the missing box and ask the clerk to correct it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try AI at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never needed an AI tool, and a small saving at work gives me no reason to put one on my phone.

say: **Lineworker signoff** stays essential even if office forms get shorter.
**Dead circuits** need test results, not tidy pages.
think: My **pay and shifts** stay secure in this mild picture.
Four months saved means I can **ignore** a small software fashion without risking our household bills.
do: **Keep** the usual meter and switching checks on line repairs.
**Return** forms that hide isolation readings before accepting them.
S0.quote: A tidy page does not make a circuit dead.
fieldNote: His **apprenticeship habits** and two-year diploma guide how he judges each line repair work order.
The **four-month reserve** supports calm without implying he can stop working now.

steps.text: Keep usual line repair and meter checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the office a route program may speed dispatch, but someone still has to reach the pole with a bucket truck. I would ask for real job times before a new repair target is set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Desk staff might be cut first, while my crew inherits their missing details. My own wage might stay the same, yet a tighter callout rota could trim extra pay that Elise and I had expected for retirement savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write down the drive, isolation and repair time on eight faults, then give the log to the supervisor. In the first year I would keep leading the crew and adjust our household saving plan only if callout income actually changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I dislike being told a screen knows a narrow lane better than the driver who has been there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the log show that the software misses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A low branch forces our truck onto the longer road to the river poles. I would write down the detour and the time before anyone gets near the broken wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the callout pay drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elise and I would postpone a planned family trip rather than draw down savings for it. I would first see the actual pay slips, because one quiet week proves very little.

say: **Bucket-truck access** must be included in any dispatch target.
**Actual job times** should be checked before shortening repairs.
think: Desk cuts could send **missing details** to the field crew.
Lost **callout pay** could slow our retirement saving even if base pay holds.
do: **Log** drive, isolation and repair times for eight faults.
**Postpone** the family trip if callout pay actually falls.
feel: **Uneasy** about targets drawn from a screen alone.
S1.quote: A low branch forces our truck onto the longer road to the river poles.
fieldNote: He watches **callout income**, because its loss would affect the household’s own retirement cushion.
He would cut a **family trip** only after pay slips show a real fall.

steps.text: Keep leading line repairs while logging eight fault times
Postpone family trip if callout pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell apprentices thinking AI arrives by 2028, but robots doing line repairs as well as people arrive about 2031. They will still need sound hand skills during the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about sixty-three when field robots turn up, and I expected to keep earning until Elise and I could afford to stop. Four months of expenses would not cover a long gap, and there are only some nearby line jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the household bills against my base pay and ask two nearby utilities about actual senior line openings. If robots cut my shifts after 2031, I would apply for a posted repair or inspection job that covers our bills; I would keep this crew working while those openings are only rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because my experience may still be valuable but fewer crew shifts would leave less pay. I would rather see a real lineworker job notice than a promise about retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for training to qualify?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the hiring utility which certificate the job requires and whether it pays for training. I would not spend our four-month cushion on a course without an opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say I am checking work options, not asking them to carry us. They have their own households to build.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches plans before line repair robots arrive around 2031.
**Apprentice hand skills** remain useful during the gap.
think: Fewer **crew shifts** could shorten my earning years.
Four months saved and **some nearby jobs** offer limited room to search.
do: **Compare** base lineworker pay with regular household bills.
**Apply** after 2031 for a posted local repair or inspection role if shifts fall and wages cover bills.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced pay, with a nearby search possible.
S2.quote: I would rather see a real lineworker job notice than a promise about retraining.
fieldNote: He prefers **posted jobs** to speculative courses and will not spend the existing reserve on training.
He does not assume his **grown children** will support his retirement.

steps.text: Keep line crew work while asking about nearby posted openings
Apply after 2031 for local bill-covering line job if shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives the company time to show what happens on a wet pole before thinking AI reaches the office in 2031. Field robots capable of the physical repair follow around 2034, so I would watch a real trial before changing my trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be near sixty-six when those robots arrive. Elise and I might have a retirement date by then, but our current four months saved do not let me call the matter settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the crew role and review retirement costs with Elise each year. In the first year after 2031 I would visit a field robot trial with an experienced coworker; if it proves safe and the employer offers paid controls practice needed for my present job, I would take the practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but patient. Five years is enough time to test a line repair robot without staking our household bills on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a safe trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the robot to stop when the isolation reading is wrong, then show the crew the fault it detected. A demonstration on a clean training pole would not settle the question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire sooner to avoid using controls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would not move a retirement date just to avoid a control panel; Elise and I would decide from what we can afford.

say: **Wet-pole trials** should be observed before field robots arrive around 2034.
**Paid controls practice** may be worthwhile if it supports current linework.
think: Our **four-month reserve** does not yet settle whether retirement by the field robot date is affordable.
do: **Keep** leading line repairs and review retirement costs yearly.
**Visit** a field robot trial after 2031 before judging the controls.
**Take** paid robot-controls practice only if trial proves safe and current job requires it.
feel: **Uneasy**, but willing to judge a proven machine.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to test a line repair robot without staking our household bills on it.
fieldNote: He remains **resistant to novelty** but leaves room for a real wet-pole test.
His **controls learning** depends on proven safety, paid instruction and a need in his current job.

steps.text: Keep line crew role while reviewing retirement costs yearly
Observe field robot trial after 2031 before deciding
Take paid robot-controls practice if trial safe and current job requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade puts thinking AI in 2036 and fully capable field robots around 2039. I would teach the apprentices to keep checking physical labels, whether a work order comes from a person or a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be around sixty-eight at the office date and might already have retired. If I am still working, the robot date is later still, so the immediate question is whether Elise and I have enough income to live on without my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my present crew work and review retirement income and bills with Elise each year. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would continue the physical switching checks and ask younger workers to record any robot order that points to a wrong switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the long runway, although the money still needs checking. A retirement date should come from our household account, not a line repair robot launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach an apprentice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would make the apprentice point to the actual switch label before touching the wire. A printed order is a clue, not permission to skip a test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children to help with retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Elise and I would work from our own income and savings before asking family for help.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes work orders before capable field robots arrive to repair lines around 2039.
**Physical switch checks** remain an apprentice skill.
think: I may be **retired** before the office change, but we must check the numbers.
If still working, my **field role** continues before robots arrive.
do: **Keep** leading repairs and review retirement income with Elise yearly.
**Continue** physical switching checks after 2036 if still employed.
feel: **Calm** about time, while checking retirement affordability.
S4.quote: A retirement date should come from our household account, not a line repair robot launch.
fieldNote: He favors **family responsibility** without assuming grown children will fund retirement.
His **long runway** makes field robots a later issue than the household’s current retirement affordability.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and review retirement income with Elise yearly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the field robot could shorten line repair shifts around 2031 while Elise and I still need the wages. Posted local work at a bill-covering rate would help more than a vague course offer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what an apprentice sees when a robot report calls a line safe. I want the line apprentice to touch the meter before trusting a sentence on a screen.

portrait: **Aaron Dubois**, 58, leads power line repairs and holds a two-year technical diploma.
He and wife Elise have **grown children**, ordinary lineworker pay, about four months saved and some nearby utility jobs.
He has **never used AI** and relies on apprenticeship habits and physical tests.
In **Steady Disruption**, he worries about callout income and checks truck times before accepting new targets.
The **2028 picture** worries him because field robots could cut earning years before retirement is affordable.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce repair shifts around 2031 while he still needs lineworker wages.
whatWouldHelp: A posted **local job** at bill-covering pay would offer an income path if crew shifts fall.
headlineQuote: I want the line apprentice to touch the meter before trusting a sentence on a screen.
